To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the privacy guarantees of differentially private algorithms can be strengthened by applying the same algorithm to the dataset a second time, (ii) the privacy guarantees can be strengthened further by applying the same algorithms to the dataset a third time, (iii) this can be done repeatedly, and (iv) the strengthened guarantees are not only stronger, but also tighter.

(i) the privacy guarantees provided by the standard composition theorem are not tight, and (ii) the Fundamental Law of Information Re- covery is a consequence of the privacy guarantees provided when the composition theorem is tightened.

(a) the Fundamental Law of Information Reconciliation is tight; (b) the Fundamental Law is a special case of the Fundamental Law of Differential Privacy; (c) the Fundamental Law can be extended to the case of approximate differential privacy; (d) the Fundamental Law applies to any privacy notion that is a special case (in the sense of Definition 2.1) of approximate differential privacy.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

we have developed the theory of “concentrated differential privacy”, which is an extension of the theory of differential privacy that allows to reason about the cumulative privacy loss over many analyses.
the Fundamental Law is not a barrier to releasing many statistics about a dataset, and in fact it may be possible to release an unbounded number of statistics while preserving privacy.

we have shown how to use differential privacy to achieve the Fundamental Law, and in fact to achieve the Fundamental law with a multiplicative factor of 2, and with a multiplicative error of at most 1.1.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the privacy guarantees of differential privacy are much more robust to composition than was previously thought.
the Fundamental Law of Information Re- covery is tight, up to logarithmic factors, for any number k of analyses.
the composition of k differentially private algorithms can be made arbitrarily more private at the cost of only a constant factor in accuracy (or, equivalently, only a constant factor increase in ε).
